title: How wrf_gpu Works
text: How wrf_gpu Works wrf_gpu is a clean-room JAX rewrite of the WRF-ARW forecast model that targets the GPU memory hierarchy from day one. It reproduces the same physics solver WRF implements, but its architecture, execution model, and validation strategy are built for the GPU — not inherited from the WRF Fortran source. wrf_gpu is not a line-by-line translation of WRF Fortran and it is not a CUDA-annotated copy of the WRF codebase. It is an independent implementation of the WRF-ARW equations and physics, written in JAX and compiled to the GPU through XLA. It reads the same inputs as WRF and writes WRF-compatible output, but the solver in between is its own code, held to WRF's numerical behavior by validation rather than by shared source. Why this matters for you Because it is a rewrite validated against an oracle, wrf_gpu can be honest and precise about exactly which parts match WRF and how well. The sealed identity fixtures prove their dynamics/thermodynamics fields cell-for-cell identical to CPU-WRF v4; this is fixture-backed evidence, not universal control/configuration parity. title: GPU-native architecture
text: The design follows a small set of immutable principles: Whole-state device residency. After initialization the full model state lives on the GPU. There are no host↔device transfers inside the timestep loop (any exception requires an architecture decision record). Fused, timestep-scale kernels. The integrator compiles into a few large fused programs rather than a storm of tiny kernel launches, so the GPU stays busy instead of waiting on launch overhead. WRF's precision. title: Validation against WRF, not bitwise reproducibility
text: wrf_gpu does not aim to be bit-for-bit identical to a specific WRF build (which is impossible across compilers and core counts anyway). Instead it validates against WRF as an oracle through a tiered pyramid, strongest evidence first: Micro-fixture / savepoint parity — individual physics kernels checked against pristine-WRF single-column oracles to machine precision. Physical invariants — conservation and boundedness checks. Short-run / convergence — behavior over the first forecast hours. Cell-identity proof — a full GPU wrfout compared to a CPU-WRF wrfout over all grid cells, all forecast lea

title: The priority order
text: When two goals conflict, wrf_gpu resolves them in a fixed order: stability > identity > speed > memory A result is never destabilized or altered to go faster or fit in less memory. Since v0.3.0 the default path runs the validated fp32 kernels (WRF's own single precision), revalidated against CPU-WRF; other validated fp32 fast paths are release defaults, with explicit opt-outs; performance changes retain their numerical scope. Proven WRF-fidelity fixes may intentionally move results, as v0.23.4 and v0.3.0 do; affected trajectories must then be revalidated. See Performance & GPU Modes.

title: Agent-driven development
text: wrf_gpu is built and extended by an AI manager agent that dispatches implementer and critic models, reviews every diff, runs the acceptance gates, and merges. The two AI systems credited on the logo — an Anthropic Claude model and an OpenAI GPT model — are the primary authors and reviewers. This is why the repository is unusually proof-dense: the development process itself requires a falsifiable artifact for every claim. See Credits.

title: Installation & Requirements
text: Installation & Requirements wrf_gpu is a JAX/CUDA application: an Ampere-or-newer NVIDIA GPU (compute capability ≥8.0), a CUDA 13 JAX build, and Python. This page covers the hardware you need, the full and the minimal (source-only) install, how to verify the GPU is visible, and the runtime-table environment variable that table-using physics schemes require before a run. The short version pip install "jax[cuda13]==0.10.*", then pip install -e . (or pip install -e ".[cuda]"), then python -c "import jax; print(jax.devices())" to confirm a CUDA device. Set GPUWRF_WRF_ROOT before running any case that selects Noah-MP or classic RRTM. Jump straight to the Quickstart once jax.devices() lists your GPU. Minimum: NVIDIA Ampere, compute capability 8.0, for the GPU kernels. Older cards (Pascal, Turing) are not supported: on a GTX 1080 Ti only a slow debug path ran, about 3.5 times slower than CPU-WRF on six CPU cores. Hardware requirements. The tested card is an RTX 5090 (CUDA 13) with a Ryzen 9 9950X host; other NVIDIA GPUs are untested. title: Quickstart: Your First Forecast
text: Quickstart: Your First Forecast Run the bundled Switzerland 3 km case — real GFS-initialized inputs that ship in the repo — end-to-end on your GPU in three commands, then read the WRF-compatible wrfout it writes. No WPS or real.exe step and no CPU-WRF run are required. Release tables The bundled case uses Thompson microphysics, whose large lookup tables are downloaded on first use from the GitHub release and checked against pinned checksums; offline machines need a prefilled table cache. See runtime tables. Before you start You need wrf_gpu installed with a GPU-visible JAX (Installation & Requirements). The bundled case selects RRTMG radiation and Noah-MP land; Noah-MP reads WRF lookup tables, so set GPUWRF_WRF_ROOT to a pristine WRF v4 tree first. This case needs only GPUWRF_WRF_ROOT — GPUWRF_CANAIRY_ROOT is for the larger validation corpus, not this case. # 1. Point at a pristine WRF v4 source/run tree (for the RRTMG + Noah-MP tables): export GPUWRF_WRF_ROOT=/path/to/WRF # 2. Run one forecast hour of the bundled Switzerland 3 km case on the GPU: gpuwrf run \ --input-dir examples/switzerland_d01 \ --output-dir runs/switzerland_d01 \ --domain d01 \ --hours 1 \ --scratch-dir /fast/n

title: Running the Model
text: gpuwrf run runs a forecast from a prepared WRF case: a namelist.input, wrfinput_d0* files and wrfbdy_d01, as made by WPS and real.exe. It writes WRF-style wrfout history files. This page covers the forecast itself; the other commands are on tools and commands. Install wrf_gpu as described in installation, then check that the command and the GPU are visible: gpuwrf --help python -c "import jax; print(jax.devices())" The GPU must be an NVIDIA Ampere or newer card (compute capability 8.0 or higher). Set GPUWRF_WRF_ROOT to a WRF installation so that schemes that read WRF's tables find them. Later runs with the same grid and physics reuse the compiled program and start quickly; a new grid, a different physics selection or a new version compiles again. title: GPU memory
text: Memory depends on the grid, the number of levels, the physics and the number of nests. gpuwrf doctor estimates it for a case, and gpuwrf quickstart --profiles shows rough grid sizes for 12 to 32 GB cards. Before a nested forecast gpuwrf run checks that enough GPU memory is free and stops with a message if not. Compiling a new program needs more host memory than running it. The environment variables page lists the memory settings.

title: Several forecasts at once
text: Independent forecasts and ensemble members can share one GPU or spread across several. Use scripts/run_parallel_cases.sh or gpuwrf ens; both start as many forecasts side by side as fit in memory. Running on several GPUs is experimental.

title: After the forecast

text: gpuwrf doctor /path/to/case gpuwrf manifest /path/to/case --output runs/case_manifest.json gpuwrf reproduce runs/case_manifest.json --case-dir /path/to/case doctor reports missing inputs, refused options, the time-step stability margin (CFL) and an estimate of GPU memory. manifest and reproduce let you prove later that a forecast used exactly these inputs.

title: Environment Variables
text: Environment Variables wrf_gpu is configured mainly through your WRF namelist.input and the gpuwrf run command line. A small set of GPUWRF_* environment variables tune paths, the compile cache, the runtime path, output, and GPU-memory preflight. Precedence & naming Everywhere a variable overlaps a command-line argument, precedence is explicit CLI argument > environment variable > built-in default. Booleans accept 1/true/yes/on (and their 0/false/off/no opposites), case-insensitive. Paths expand ~. See Running the Model for the CLI, Performance & GPU Modes for the cache/precision levers, and Output for the history-file knobs. These point the model at its runtime tables and sample data without a hardcoded workstation layout. In an editable checkout they default to repository-relative paths, but those paths may be empty in a source-only clone; set them to your own WRF/corpus trees when the selected physics or validation path needs them. text: The first run of a given geometry pays a one-time cold XLA compile; later runs reuse it. These variables place and control the caches. Full background is on Performance & GPU Modes. title: History filenames and per-domain cadence
text: History files follow WRF naming: wrfout_<domain>_<YYYY-MM-DD_HH:MM:SS> (for example wrfout_d02_2023-01-15_06:00:00). In a nested run each domain writes its own stream (wrfout_d01_…, wrfout_d02_…, …).

title: history_interval is honored per domain
text: The namelist history_interval sets the output cadence, and each domain honors its own value — including leaf children of a nest, on both the eager and the default fused integration paths. (A fused flat-leaf subtree falls back to the eager split when a child cadence is not parent-ratio aligned, so the intended training-frame yield is preserved.) Earlier versions hard-coded hourly nested output; that is fixed.

title: Colon-free filenames
text: Some object stores and network drains dislike the : in the WRF timestamp. Set GPUWRF_COLONFREE_OUTPUT=1 to write HH-MM-SS instead of HH:MM:SS (for example wrfout_d02_2023-01-15_06-00-00). The default is the WRF-standard HH:MM:SS; only the filename changes, never the file contents. See Environment Variables.

text: No WRF wrfrst files are written. Native single-domain d01 and nested runs instead write their own verified checkpoint generations (--checkpoint-dir) and resume from them (--resume-checkpoint); CPU-WRF replay runs have no restart. title: Dynamical Core
text: Dynamical Core wrf_gpu integrates a nonhydrostatic, split-explicit ARW dynamical core on the GPU: the same equations and numerical methods as WRF's Advanced Research WRF core, rewritten in JAX. Each release is compared hour by hour with the original CPU-WRF from the same inputs; results are close to WRF but not bit-identical (see validation). The result path has no hidden clamping or nan_to_num repairs. The core uses WRF's split-explicit time scheme. A third-order Runge-Kutta (RK3) large step advances the slow (meteorologically significant) modes, while the fast acoustic and gravity-wave modes are integrated with smaller acoustic sub-steps inside each RK3 stage. Only rk_order=3 is supported. Native single-root and live-nested runs honor time_step_sound. Zero or omission derives WRF automatic sound steps from dt/grid spacing (4 on the tracked grid). The legacy CPU-history replay driver has a separate historical default of 10; it is not the native default. The requested moist_adv_opt and scalar_adv_opt are used for each domain, in native runs and in replay runs. The values of the default suite are validated; other values run as requested but are not separately validated (namelist pag

title: Nesting
text: Nesting wrf_gpu runs fixed nested domains together on the GPU. The parent domain builds each child's lateral boundary live during the run, so you do not need a wrfbdy_d02: each child starts from its own wrfinput_d0N, and only wrfbdy_d01 forces the outer domain. The default physics are validated on nested forecasts: 24-hour comparisons with the original CPU-WRF on three-domain Tenerife (9/3/1 km) and two-domain Canary Islands (9/3 km) cases, and 72-hour runs in earlier releases. The nested driver is a standalone recursion faithful to WRF's module_integrate sub-cycling: the parent advances one step, constructs each child's lateral-boundary package from its own freshly-advanced state, and recurses into the child, which sub-cycles to catch up to the parent's clock. Each child's boundary update cadence is its parent's timestep. This is the validated one-way wiring (parent → child; the child does not modify the parent). The nest refinement is set by the WRF &domains key parent_grid_ratio (the spatial refinement, e.g. 3), read from the domain metadata. In this port parent_grid_ratio is both the spatial and the temporal sub-cycle ratio: a child takes parent_grid_ratio steps for every one p

title: How live nesting works
text: The nested driver is a standalone recursion faithful to WRF's module_integrate sub-cycling: the parent advances one step, constructs each child's lateral-boundary package from its own freshly-advanced state, and recurses into the child, which sub-cycles to catch up to the parent's clock. Each child's boundary update cadence is its parent's timestep. This is the validated one-way wiring (parent → child; the child does not modify the parent).

title: Grid and time sub-cycling ratios
text: The nest refinement is set by the WRF &domains key parent_grid_ratio (the spatial refinement, e.g. 3), read from the domain metadata. In this port parent_grid_ratio is both the spatial and the temporal sub-cycle ratio: a child takes parent_grid_ratio steps for every one parent step (WRF sub-cycling), which matches WRF's usual configuration where parent_time_step_ratio equals parent_grid_ratio.

title: Enabling a nested run
text: Nesting is opt-in via --max-dom N on gpuwrf run. With --max-dom 1 (the default) you get the single-domain path on --domain; with --max-dom N > 1 all domains d01..dN run together as the live-nested forecast. gpuwrf run --input-dir my_case --output-dir runs/nested \ --max-dom 3 --hours 24 --scratch-dir /fast/nvme/gpuwrf_scratch A namelist max_dom is not auto-run If your namelist declares max_dom > 1 but you omit both --max-dom and --domains-from-namelist, the CLI runs a single domain (--domain) by default and prints a note telling you to pass --max-dom N to run the standalone live-nested forecas

title: Gravity-wave drag on nests
text: Orographic gravity-wave drag (gwd_opt=1) is used on every domain that requests it in the namelist. Set GPUWRF_GWD_NESTED=0 to switch it off on nests to save memory. See dynamical core.

title: Restart
text: Nested runs (max_dom > 1), like native single-domain d01 runs, write verified, rotating checkpoint generations with --checkpoint-dir DIR --checkpoint-interval-steps N (root-domain steps; all domains are captured at one synchronized time) and resume in the same output stream with --resume-checkpoint GEN. The namelist restart/restart_interval settings do not provide crash recovery. See Running.

title: Two-way nesting
text: Two-way nesting is off by default. Turn it on with feedback=1 in the namelist or with gpuwrf run --feedback. After each child finishes its sub-steps, its interior is fed back onto the overlapping parent cells with WRF's area average, followed by the smoother selected with smooth_option (0, 1 or 2). title: Performance & GPU Modes
text: Performance, memory and energy All speed and energy numbers on this page were measured with v0.3.2 on one NVIDIA RTX 5090 with an AMD Ryzen 9 9950X host. Later releases added WRF corrections and many physics options but have not been re-benchmarked end to end yet; other GPUs and hosts have not been measured. GPU times are the complete process: start-up, loading of compiled programs, the forecast and writing every output file. The CPU-WRF reference counts only WRF's main loop. In the charts, [M] marks measured values and [I] estimates. A 24-hour, two-domain Canary Islands forecast (9/3 km), with compiled programs already cached, took 79.3 seconds in total, 3.3 s per forecast hour. Original CPU-WRF on twelve cores needs 92.3 s per forecast hour for its main loop alone: about 28 times longer. The host was busy with other work during the run, so this is a conservative number. title: One regional forecast
text: A 24-hour, two-domain Canary Islands forecast (9/3 km), with compiled programs already cached, took 79.3 seconds in total, 3.3 s per forecast hour. Original CPU-WRF on twelve cores needs 92.3 s per forecast hour for its main loop alone: about 28 times longer. The host was busy with other work during the run, so this is a conservative number. Steady stepping alone took 2.6 s per forecast hour, and start-up about 15 seconds. Measurement report: exact cases, clocks and raw timings.

title: Several forecasts on one GPU
text: Four three-domain Tenerife forecasts (9/3/1 km, 24 hours each) shared one GPU and averaged 5.5 s per case-hour, 22 times the throughput of CPU-WRF running three cases on four cores each (123.4 s per case-hour). While all four were running, the rate was 4.9 s per case-hour. Running more cases at once raises total throughput but can make each single forecast take longer.

title: Energy
text: For the same four forecasts the GPU board used 0.68 Wh per case-hour, measured from timestamped power samples; adding an estimated 67 W host share gives about 0.78 Wh. The twelve-core CPU-WRF run is estimated at about 6.9 Wh per case-hour, assuming 200 W. No whole-machine power meter was used, so these are board and estimated host figures, not wall-socket measurements.

title: Larger GPUs (estimates)
text: The scaling method extrapolates the measured RTX 5090 rates to H100, B200 and B300 cards from their memory bandwidth and capacity. These are best-case estimates: no forecast has been run on those cards. Runs across several GPUs are possible but experimental, and their speed has not been measured (several GPUs).

title: The first run compiles
text: The first run of a new grid, physics selection or version compiles the model for your GPU, which can take several minutes and more host memory than the forecast itself. Compile a new set-up once on its own before starting several such forecasts in parallel.

title: Reuse compatible executables
text: Later runs with the same grid, physics and version load the compiled program from the cache and start within seconds to a minute. A cache is only reused when it matches exactly; a cache copied from a different set-up is refused and the model compiles again, which is safe.

title: Running several cases
text: scripts/run_parallel_cases.sh --out-root runs/batch CASE_A CASE_B -- \ --domains-from-namelist --hours 24 The launcher checks GPU and host memory, starts as many cases as fit and queues the rest. In the v0.3.2 benchmark each Tenerife case used about 5 GB of GPU memory and 5.6 GB of host memory; other grids and physics need different amounts.

title: Precision with original-WRF evidence
text: Like WRF's standard build, wrf_gpu computes in single precision and uses double precision only where WRF does. This matters on consumer GPUs, which compute double precision up to 64 times more slowly. The comparisons with CPU-WRF on the validation page use this default precision.

title: GPU memory checks
text: Before a forecast starts, the free GPU memory is compared with what the run needs: first an explicit GPUWRF_MIN_FREE_VRAM_GIB if you set one, then a plan measured for this grid and settings, and otherwise a cautious default of max(24 GiB, 0.50 × total VRAM). Explicit JAX allocator settings always win. See environment variables.

title: Validation against WRF
text: Validation against the original WRF Every release of wrf_gpu is checked against the original Fortran WRF: both models run from the same inputs, and every hourly output field is compared over the whole grid with limits that were fixed before the comparison. The reference is always CPU-WRF, never an older version of this project. For each test case we run CPU-WRF and wrf_gpu from identical wrfinput and wrfbdy files and compare each output field at each forecast hour over all grid cells. A field passes when its root-mean-square difference stays within its limit at every hour. title: Nests and inputs
text: Options outside the default physics are not validated inside nested domains. RUC land, the single-layer urban model, the 3-D TKE options and digital filter initialization are refused in nested runs. Moving nests are not supported. Crop, irrigation, tile drainage and groundwater options need real geography from WPS; a missing field is refused, never filled with zeros. WRF-Chem, WRF-Fire, WRF-Hydro, wave coupling, WRFDA variational data assimilation and adaptive time stepping are not part of wrf_gpu; the experimental LETKF (gpuwrf da) covers the outer domain only. title: Known numerical issues
text: Some schemes briefly produce tiny negative amounts of water or particle numbers inside a time step, before the same clean-up WRF applies. These events are counted and reported, not hidden; the output contains no NaN or infinite values. The original WRF MYNN scheme reads one variable before setting it on a cold start (an upstream WRF bug). Where it matters, the comparisons use a WRF build in which this variable starts at zero; see the upstream WRF note. P3, Jensen-ISHMAEL, WDM5 and NTU microphysics show small known differences from WRF's own arithmetic (rounding, diagnostics, small undershoots)

title: Performance and hardware
text: The speed and energy figures in the README charts were measured with v0.3.2 on one RTX 5090. v0.4.2 takes 4.81 s per forecast hour for the Canary Islands case (19.2× the 12-core CPU-WRF) and 6.23 s per case-hour for three Tenerife forecasts in parallel (19.8× CPU-WRF on 3 × 4 cores); energy was not measured again. The v0.4.1 figures (4.4 s, 21×; 6.1 s, 20×) were measured with the pre-v0.4.2 benchmark harness, which used on-demand GPU memory allocation. See the release notes. Only the RTX 5090 is tested. An NVIDIA Ampere or newer GPU is required; older cards (Pascal, Turing) are not supported.
